headline.en: Every voice has an easy note. There's no wrong one.

detail.en: Not too high, not too low

text.en: Sing any note that feels easy, and hold it for a few seconds.
Every voice has an easy note, and there's no wrong one. Hum any note that feels easy, softly on "oo", and hold it for a few seconds. No push, no strain.

headline.en: Listen, then sing the same note back.

detail.en: Hear the note all the way through

text.en: Sing along with the note.
Listen, then sing it back. Every try counts, and matching counts most.

headline.en: A note sits above or below your easy note.

detail.en: Up or down from your note?
In your head, before you sing
Higher or lower, as you heard

text.en: Listen, then sing each note back.

headline.en: Breath that's steady gives notes that are steady. Keep everything easy: stop if anything tightens or hurts.

detail.en: Let your belly and lower ribs widen
If they rise, the breath is too high
Slowly, for as long as is comfortable

text.en: Breathe in, then hold this long note on "oo".
Your vocal folds open and close once for every wave of a note: about 110 times a second in a typical man's speaking voice, about 210 in a woman's.
The unit's challenge: listen, then sing all five notes back.

headline.en: A steady note doesn't wobble or slide.

detail.en: Right on the note, no scoop

text.en: Listen, then hold the note for four beats.
Now six beats. Breathe low first.
Now eight beats, steady to the end.

headline.en: Singers have tuned to drones for centuries, from Indian classical music to choir warm-ups.

detail.en: A slow wobble means close. When it stops, you match

text.en: Hold your note with the drone under it.

measures.en: Scored on your note against the drone. The wobble slows as you get closer, and stops when you match.

headline.en: Your mouth moves; the pitch stays.

text.en: Listen, then sing the three vowels on one note.
The unit's challenge: hold your note for eight beats against the drone.
Across the world's music, melodies move mostly by small steps like these; leaps are far rarer.

headline.en: Most tunes move by step: up or down to the next note.

text.en: Listen, then sing the steps up.
Listen, then sing the steps down.

headline.en: A jump skips a note. Hear the landing first.

detail.en: In your head, before you sing

text.en: Listen, then sing the jumps.
Beethoven was almost totally deaf when his Ninth Symphony, with this tune, was first played in 1824. Today it's the European Union's anthem.

source.en: Britannica, Symphony No. 9 in D Minor

text.en: The unit's challenge: the opening of Ode to Joy, which moves by step. Listen, then sing it.

headline.en: In a song, each syllable sits on a note. Some stretch over two.

detail.en: Each on its note, some held over two

text.en: Sing the first line of Amazing Grace with the guide.

headline.en: A phrase is one breath's worth of song.

detail.en: Not in the middle of a word

text.en: Sing two lines of Amazing Grace, breathing between them.
John Newton, a slave-ship captain who became a clergyman, wrote these words for his New Year's Day sermon in 1773. They met this tune in print in 1835.
The unit's challenge: record the melody of Amazing Grace, verse 1.

headline.en: Harmony is two notes at once.

text.en: Find each note over the drone: the same, then mi above, then la below.
Hear them over the drone, then sing them with it.
Now just the drone: the same note, then above, then below.

headline.en: A third is the sweetest harmony.

title.en: Mi above do is a third

text.en: Find mi above the drone. It waits for you.
Hear mi over the drone, then sing it with the drone.
Now just the drone: sing the third above it.
The third below: hear la under the drone, then sing it.
Now just the drone: sing the third below it.

Are You Sleeping is the French round Frère Jacques. A manuscript of canons from the 1700s, in France's national library, credits it to the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau; whether he wrote it is still debated.

headline.en: In a round, the harmony happens by itself.

detail.en: The same words, the same notes
The harmony comes on its own

text.en: Learn the 2nd voice of Are You Sleeping, which starts two bars after the 1st.
Now on your own: sing the 2nd voice's first line over the chords. Keep your own words.

measures.en: Scored on your line over the chords.

text.en: Learn the alto of Michael, Row the Boat Ashore: mostly a third below the tune, landing on the note below do at the ends.
Now on your own: sing the alto's first line over the chords. Listen to the chords, not the tune.
The unit's challenge: record the 2nd voice of Are You Sleeping.

headline.en: The chords change; your note stays.

text.en: Hold your note as the chords move.

headline.en: The bass is the floor the others stand on.

detail.en: The note the chord is named after
The bass leaps from root to root

text.en: Learn the bass of Amazing Grace, for 3 singers. Too low? Sing it an octave up. We'll still light your notes.
Now on your own: sing the bass's third line over the chords. Big jumps, root to root.
"Tenor" comes from the Latin for "to hold": in medieval music, the tenor held the main tune, often in long notes.
Learn the tenor of Amazing Grace. It keeps coming back to do, the home note, while the chords change around it, just as you held your note.
Now on your own: sing the tenor's first line over the chords, and keep coming back home.

title.en: Record the bass of Amazing Grace

text.en: The unit's challenge: record the bass of Amazing Grace.

headline.en: Listen to how your parts sit together.

title.en: Listen for one that stands out

text.en: Sing the alto of Amazing Grace with the other parts.
In 1951 Les Paul layered take after take of Mary Ford's voice on one tape for "How High the Moon", nine weeks a US number one. You've just done the same.

source.en: Sound on Sound, Classic Tracks: How High The Moon

title.en: All four parts of Amazing Grace

text.en: The unit's challenge: record all four parts of Amazing Grace, one at a time.

headline.en: Expression is how you sing, not just which notes.

title.en: Get softer at a line's end

text.en: Sing this phrase, starting strong and ending soft.

headline.en: Vibrato often comes on its own when the breath is steady and the throat is easy. If it doesn't yet, that's fine: a straight tone is beautiful too.

title.en: Let it move if it wants

detail.en: A gentle wave, on its own

text.en: Find each note and hold it, relaxed.
Listen, then hold each long note steady and easy.

measures.en: Scored on the notes. Vibrato isn't graded: a straight tone is beautiful too.

headline.en: High notes like room. Only go as high as is easy, and stop if anything tightens.

text.en: Climb on "ah", opening the vowel as you go up.

measures.en: Scored on the notes. The vowels are for you to hear: listen back.

text.en: Now on "ee": let it lean toward "ih" at the top.

measures.en: Scored on the notes. The vowels are for you to hear: listen back.

headline.en: A phrase is a breath with a shape.

text.en: Sing it in one breath, growing to the top and settling at the end.

text.en: The tune was first printed in 1855, with no name. Known later as the Londonderry Air, it took Frederic Weatherly's "Danny Boy" words in 1913.
The unit's challenge: record the melody of Danny Boy, shaping each line: a breath before it, growing to its top, settling at the end.

measures.en: Scored on the notes. The shape is for you to feel: listen back.
